sources.entry: A Python implementation of a Python bytecode runner

summary.title: A Python Interpreter Written in Python (500 Lines or Less)
summary.one_liner: You learn how the CPython bytecode interpreter works by building up a stack-based toy interpreter and then reading real Python bytecode with the dis module, as used in the Byterun project.
keywords: how does the python interpreter work
virtual machine stack vs register machine
how loops and if statements compile to bytecode
takeaways: The interpreter is the last step of execution: lexing, parsing and compiling produce code objects containing bytecode that the interpreter runs.
A stack-based interpreter can be built from a few instruction methods (LOAD_VALUE, ADD_TWO_VALUES, PRINT_ANSWER) dispatched via getattr.
Python's dis module disassembles bytecode, showing how if statements and while loops are implemented with conditional and absolute jumps.
Frames live on a call stack, each with its own data stack and block stack; RETURN_VALUE passes values between frames.
summary.summary: The chapter, written by Allison Kaptur for the 500 Lines or Less book, explains how the Python interpreter works by walking through Byterun, a Python interpreter implemented in Python. It starts with a minimal stack machine that handles three instructions, then adds variables with STORE_NAME and LOAD_NAME and uses getattr-based dispatch. It then switches to real CPython bytecode, using cond.__code__.co_code and the dis module to read how conditionals and loops become jump instructions. The text ends by introducing frames, the call stack, and the data and block stacks.
